rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Parables” here convey facts about the afterlife and unseen world in forms meant to warn people.
rows.anchor: facts and realities of the hereafter and of the unknown world that are presented in the form of parables

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Human” refers to the contentious Quraysh; the general term expresses the author’s aversion to them.
rows.anchor: refers to the quarrelsome Quraysh that are already under discussion. A general word has been used in order to express aversion from them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word “qibalan” means appearing from the front or face to face.
rows.anchor: means “from the front” and “face to face.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an has fully warned the Quraysh, yet those evading reality invent excuses and will not believe or seek forgiveness until prior peoples’ fate recurs or punishment confronts them.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ān has warned them in various ways and nothing is hidden; however, people who want to evade the reality find various excuses for this.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an offers guidance while they demand punishment; when punishment descends, it will devastate them, leaving no remedy.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ān is inviting them to divine fodder but they are demanding divine punishment. There is no remedy for such wretched people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Demanding punishment from messengers is baseless and amounts to trying to defeat truth by evil.
rows.anchor: It is absolutely baseless for these people to demand this from their messengers and is tantamount to defeating truth through evil.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disputants fail to understand torment and the afterlife and mock the warnings and God’s punishment.
rows.anchor: have not understood the reality of torment and of the hereafter. They have made fun of the verses of warning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite their conduct, the Quraysh are spared through God’s mercy, while their evil deeds have barred their faculties from accepting Qur’anic guidance.
rows.anchor: it is purely because of God’s mercy. However, because of their evil deeds, their faculties have been barred from accepting guidance from the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic construction omits words before “an” by grammatical ellipsis and, through parallelism, omits “to hear it” after “in their ears.”
rows.anchor: in accordance with linguistic principles of Arabic. Similarly, on the basis of parallelism, words like

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since their faculties will not respond, the Prophet should consign their case to God and patiently complete his duty of conveying the truth conclusively.
rows.anchor: consign their matter to God and patiently continue to discharge his obligation so that the truth is fully communicated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word “maw’il” means a place of refuge.
rows.anchor: The word ﻣَﻮۡ means “a place of refuge.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s mercy explains the wrongdoers’ respite: He has appointed a time to seize them, and then they will find nowhere to escape.
rows.anchor: He is in no haste for He has appointed a time to grab them. When the time comes, they will not be able to escape

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The destroyed towns provide historical evidence for the preceding warning about God’s appointed punishment.
rows.anchor: This verse presents historical evidence on what is said earlier.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account completes the preceding instruction for the Prophet to be patient with his arrogant enemies.
rows.anchor: In the succeeding verses, this topic is brought to completion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the surah’s climax, patience is an active virtue on which rights and duties toward God and people depend.
rows.anchor: patience is not a negative attitude. It is a positive reality. It is on it that all rights thrive and sustain.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Patience rests on belief that everything occurs by God’s permission and will, down to the movement of a particle.
rows.anchor: whatever happens in this world happens because of God’s permission and under His will and intention.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is good and wise: respite for wrongdoers serves a good purpose, while hardship for the righteous can open a beneficial way.
rows.anchor: If He gives respite to evildoers, it is not because He loves them or is helpless before them. In this respite too, He wants to nourish a great good.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human knowledge is limited, so people should patiently and gratefully perform their duties; the wisdom of God’s decisions will be fully disclosed in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: All the secrets of these intentions will only stand revealed in the hereafter. The right attitude for human beings in this world is that they should be patient and grateful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ educational journey illustrates divine wisdom more forcefully than abstract explanation; God sent him to a specially taught servant to learn submission to divine decisions.
rows.anchor: The way these secrets of wisdom become evident through incidents is much more powerful than mere statements.

rows.speaker: our exegetes
rows.claim: A narrative says Moses claimed to be the most knowledgeable person, so God sent him to someone more knowledgeable as a reprimand.
rows.anchor: our exegetes have relied on a strange narrative while explaining this incident. According to this narrative, once Moses (sws) audaciously claimed that at that time he was the most knowledgeable person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Moses’ statement was arrogant and earned reprimand is baseless: prophets declare knowledge from God, and this account’s real purpose is his education in divine wisdom.
rows.anchor: arrogance or he be regarded worthy of reprimand for saying this. So why should Moses (sws) deserve this treatment? Nevertheless, in my opinion this occasion of revelation is totally baseless

none: This segment contains only the text and translation of verses 18:60-82.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He translates “fatā” as “student,” since the word implies both youth and a student-attendant relationship; Moses treats him as a companion, not merely a servant.
rows.anchor: I have translated the word t as “student” instead of “servant” or “young man.” Incorporated in this word is both the young age and nature of relationship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The meeting point of the seas was most probably where the Gulf of Aqabah and the Suez Canal meet, from where Moses spent phases of his life with the Israelites.
rows.anchor: The meeting place of the two seas is most probably the point where the gulf of ‘Aqabah and the Suez canal meet.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ḥuqab” can mean an era, a year, or a period of eighty years or longer.
rows.anchor: means “an era of time”, “year”, “a period of eighty years or even more.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses was divinely instructed to travel and spoke with such resolve that he would reach the destination or die on the way; his student could accompany him if able.
rows.anchor: Moses (sws) must have been divinely asked to undertake this journey. He expressed this desire before his student.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word for the fish’s path is explained as water flowing away from a vessel.
rows.anchor: The word Ê means “flowing away of water from a utensil.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account suppresses part of the journey: the pair rested at the seas’ meeting point, left the fish intended for breakfast, and later retraced their steps to retrieve it.
rows.anchor: Both journeyed and reached the meeting place of the seas. Here they rested in the valley of a mountain for some time.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The extraordinary fish escape made the student fear Moses would disbelieve and rebuke him, so he hesitated to report it; Moses likely thought the student had taken the fish.
rows.anchor: The student now had no option but to reveal the truth to Moses (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ghadā’” means breakfast and “naṣab” means fatigue; the wording is unsuitable for raw or living fish and indicates the fish had been roasted, before Moses asks for food after tiring travel.
rows.anchor: This word is not appropriate at all for non-roasted fish or fish that is alive. It is a clear indication that the fish was roasted.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The student had to disclose the truth; “ara’ayta” signals hesitation, like “what should I say,” while blaming Satan politely apologizes for his lapse.
rows.anchor: It is like saying “what should I say ...” or “just look and see ...”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Expecting a rebuke, the student explained what happened, but Moses recognized the place as the meeting point with the servant he had been instructed to find and turned back.
rows.anchor: Moses (sws) jumped to the news since it was at this place where he had been instructed to meet a servant of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an leaves the specially blessed, knowledgeable servant unnamed, describing only his attributes; some narratives identify him as Khidr.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ān has not named this individual. It has only mentioned some particular attributes he possessed. In some narratives, he has been

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because he sees no reason to reject the narratives, the author adopts the name Khidr for the unnamed servant.
rows.anchor: Since I do not find any reason to reject these narratives, I shall adopt this name.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author considers Khidr a prophet: first, a messenger such as Moses would not appropriately be sent to a non-prophet for instruction.
rows.anchor: a celebrated prophet in fact messenger as Moses (sws) was sent to him for instruction and to gain knowledge.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr’s absence from the Qur’an and Torah by name is no objection, since neither scripture names every prophet; each prophet has a particular superiority, and Moses learning from Khidr does not establish Khidr’s absolute superiority.
rows.anchor: has not mentioned many prophets. Same is the case with the Torah too.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reason Khidr was a prophet is that his Qur’anic attributes and his claim that his acts were not his own will indicate divine revelation and knowledge of God’s secrets.
rows.anchor: All these aspects show that he was a prophet of God who received His revelations. He also had the distinction that God had revealed some of His secrets to him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Rushd” means knowledge and wisdom, here Khidr’s special knowledge of the universe’s hidden wisdom.
rows.anchor: means “knowledge and wisdom.” However, here it means the special knowledge given to Khiḍr by the Almighty about the secrets of the universe.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr warns Moses that he will find some acts abhorrent because Moses cannot perceive their hidden wisdom and therefore will not be patient.
rows.anchor: there will be certain things he will do that would be very abhorrent to him and he would not be able to exercise patience.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses promises Khidr that he will remain patient and never disobey him.
rows.anchor: Moses (sws) promised Khiḍr that he would stay patient and never disobey him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Moses’ commitment, Khidr permits him to accompany him under the stated condition.
rows.anchor: After the commitment given by Moses (sws), Khi ḍr allowed him to accompany him on the condition stated.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Imr” means something strange and abhorrent.
rows.anchor: The word ﻣۡﺮً means something strange and abhorrent.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Irhāq” means burdening someone beyond what they can bear or inflicting hardship; the phrase means causing difficulty.
rows.anchor: to burden someone with more than what he can bear or to inflict hardships on someone. Thus

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After his second outburst, Moses apologizes and says he will stop accompanying Khidr if he questions him again.
rows.anchor: Once again Moses (sws) apologized for his outburst and said that next time he would stop accompanying him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses again could not restrain himself at the incident involving the wall.
rows.anchor: Again Moses (sws) could not restrain himself at the incident mentioned in the verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr announces the parting because Moses’ education is complete after the third incident, not because the truth has been conclusively conveyed to him.
rows.anchor: he had not declared this because the truth had been conclusively conveyed to Moses (sws); the fact was that with this third incident his education and instruction too stood completed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king was probably forcibly confiscating ships for a war campaign.
rows.anchor: It seems that the king was forcibly confiscating ships for most probably for a war campaign.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ship illustrates that losses suffered by the poor and righteous conceal a benefit, so they should patiently accept God’s wise decisions even when they cannot understand them.
rows.anchor: This is an example of the fact that if in this world the poor and the righteous are inflicted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word “raḥm” means affection, sympathy, and concern.
rows.anchor: means “affection, sympathy and concern.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A calamity for believers hides a great benefit known only to God; they should remain patient and will recognize the wisdom when it becomes clear.
rows.anchor: Thus believers should exercise patience. When they become aware of it, they will understand God’s wisdom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ companion clarifies that he did none of the acts from his own opinion; God’s concessions to wrongdoers serve a hidden expediency and complete the case against them while advancing truth for its adherents.
rows.anchor: these miscreants only complete God’s conclusive argument against them. However, through them God furthers the cause of the adherents of truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story’s secondary lesson is that wisdom is granted to true seekers who exert themselves, travel, yearn for knowledge, and sacrifice ego and other desires.
rows.anchor: Those who want to acquire it must work very hard for it. It is not obtained by just sitting at home; it needs a lot of effort and struggle.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sharī‘ah is the real guide: even a great guide such as Khidr must be challenged when an act appears to violate it; Moses accepted the acts only after learning they followed God’s directives, already disclosed to him by revelation.
rows.anchor: our real guide is the sharī‘ah. It is our obligation that we follow it in all circumstances. If we see anything against it, we must disregard it even if it is done by as great a guide as Khiḍr.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the view that Quṭubs and Abdāls exist in every age as authorities beyond sharī‘ah; these terms lack Qur’anic or hadith basis, and no one may claim license to violate the law.
rows.anchor: I regard as baseless the view of all those who think that there exist some Quṭub and Abdāl in every age like Khiḍr

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s will is known through revelation in the Book and the Messenger’s practice; an alleged Khidr who kills today would face qiṣāṣ, since no such authority exists in sharī‘ah.
rows.anchor: directives is through His Book and the practice of His messenger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account raises why Khidr attributes the ship to his own intention, the boy’s case to “we,” and the wall to God’s will, despite saying his acts were not his own.
rows.anchor: why did he use different styles to say the same thing? When he has ascribed all his doings to God’s directive, then the clear style for this was

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a person’s will accords with God’s, an act may be attributed to either; rhetorical etiquette assigns the apparently bad act of damaging a ship to Khidr, while the good act of preserving orphans’ treasure is attributed to God.
rows.anchor: when a person’s will matches the will of God, he can ascribe it to God as well as to himself. The difference has much to do with the requisites of eloquence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr’s plural “we” represents all who implement God’s will, since he acted as an instrument of that will in the universe.
rows.anchor: when on such an instances, a speaker uses the plural, he represents the statement of all members of the category that he stands for or is their instrument of implementation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We feared” expresses Khidr’s own deduction, not fear attributed to God: revelation told him to kill the believing parents’ son, and he inferred the boy would oppress them, though that reason was not specified in the revelation.
rows.anchor: is not in relation to God. It has been used by him to show that he had exercised his own opinion.
